section.title: The Raising of Lazarus
section.sectionRationale: The seventh and greatest sign brings the Book of Signs to its climax. Jesus deliberately delays, lets His friend Lazarus die, then raises him after four days in the tomb, declaring, I am the resurrection and the life. The sign both reveals Jesus as the conqueror of death and, ironically, seals His own death, as the Sanhedrin resolves to kill Him, and Caiaphas unwittingly prophesies that one man must die for the people.
section.thesis: Jesus, who is Himself the resurrection and the life, weeps at the grave of His friend and then calls him out of the tomb after four days, revealing the glory of God and giving a sign that He is the Christ who conquers death, even as the raising of Lazarus sets in motion the plot that will bring Jesus to His own death for the people.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the news of Lazarus's sickness and Jesus' deliberate delay; the meeting with Martha and the great claim, I am the resurrection and the life; Jesus weeping with Mary at the grave; the raising of Lazarus from the tomb; and the Sanhedrin's plot and Caiaphas's unwitting prophecy.

units.label: The death of Lazarus
units.note: this sickness is for the glory of God

verses.text: At this time a man named Lazarus was sick. He lived in Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.
(Mary, whose brother Lazarus was sick, was to anoint the Lord with perfume and wipe His feet with her hair.)
So the sisters sent word to Jesus, “Lord, the one You love is sick.”
When Jesus heard this, He said, “This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.
So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days,
and then He said to the disciples, “Let us go back to Judea.”
“Rabbi,” they replied, “the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?”
Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? If anyone walks in the daytime, he will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world.
But if anyone walks at night, he will stumble, because he has no light.”
After He had said this, He told them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up.”
His disciples replied, “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better.”
They thought that Jesus was talking about actual sleep, but He was speaking about the death of Lazarus.
So Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus is dead,
and for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”
Then Thomas called Didymus said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.”

units.label: I am the resurrection and the life

verses.text: When Jesus arrived, He found that Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, a little less than two miles away,
and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them in the loss of their brother.
So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home.
Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.
But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him.”
“Your brother will rise again,” Jesus told her.
Martha replied, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “{{egoeimi|I am}} the {{anastasis|resurrection}} and the {{zoe|life}}. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.
And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?”
“Yes, Lord,” she answered, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.”
After Martha had said this, she went back and called her sister Mary aside to tell her, “The Teacher is here and is asking for you.”
And when Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to Him.
Now Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still at the place where Martha had met Him.
When the Jews who were in the house consoling Mary saw how quickly she got up and went out, they followed her, supposing she was going to the tomb to mourn there.
When Mary came to Jesus and saw Him, she fell at His feet and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”
When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
“Where have you put him?” He asked. “Come and see, Lord,” they answered.
Jesus wept.
Then the Jews said, “See how He loved him!”
But some of them asked, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?”
Jesus, once again deeply moved, came to the tomb. It was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance.
“Take away the stone,” Jesus said. “Lord, by now he stinks,” said Martha, the sister of the dead man. “It has already been four days.”
Jesus replied, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the {{doxa|glory}} of God?”
So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me.
I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.”
After Jesus had said this, He called out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
The man who had been dead came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth. “Unwrap him and let him go,” Jesus told them.

units.label: The plot to kill Jesus
units.note: one man must die for the people

verses.text: Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in Him.
But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
Then the chief priests and Pharisees convened the Sanhedrin and said, “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs.
If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”
But one of them, named Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all!
You do not realize that it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish.”
Caiaphas did not say this on his own. Instead, as high priest that year, he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation,
and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one.
So from that day on they plotted to kill Him.
As a result, Jesus no longer went about publicly among the Jews, but He withdrew to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness. And He stayed there with the disciples.
Now the Jewish Passover was near, and many people went up from the country to Jerusalem to purify themselves before the Passover.
They kept looking for Jesus and asking one another as they stood in the temple courts, “What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?”
But the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. In the fifth great I am saying, Jesus tells Martha, I am the resurrection and the life. He does not merely promise resurrection at the last day; He is Himself resurrection and life in person, so that the future hope becomes present in Him. To be joined to Him by faith is to have life that death cannot end.

anastasis.gloss: Resurrection, a rising up from the dead. Martha believed in a resurrection at the last day; Jesus reveals that the resurrection is not only an event but a person, Himself. The raising of Lazarus is a foretaste and pledge, a sign pointing to Jesus' own resurrection and to the final rising of all who are His.

zoe.gloss: Life. Jesus is the life, the source of the very life of God, so that whoever believes in Him will live even though he dies, and whoever lives and believes will never finally die. The word gathers up John's insistence that eternal life is found in the Son and cannot be undone by the grave.

doxa.gloss: Glory, the revealed splendor of God. Jesus says the sickness is for the glory of God and promises Martha she will see the glory of God if she believes. The raising of Lazarus displays that glory, and in John it points beyond itself to the greater glory of the cross and resurrection, the hour toward which this sign hastens Jesus.

basic.context: Lazarus, whom Jesus loved, falls sick, and his sisters send word. Strangely, Jesus stays where He is two more days, and Lazarus dies. When Jesus finally comes, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Him with grief and faith, and Jesus tells her, I am the resurrection and the life. At the grave, surrounded by weeping, Jesus Himself weeps, then commands the stone removed and calls, Lazarus, come out, and the dead man walks out still wrapped in grave clothes. Many believe, but the leaders, alarmed, resolve to kill Jesus, and Caiaphas says, without knowing its full truth, that one man should die for the people.
basic.hermeneutics: The delay is deliberate, not neglect; Jesus loves the family and waits so that a greater glory may be revealed. The key claim is I am the resurrection and the life, which lifts resurrection from a distant event to a present person. Jesus' tears show that His power over death does not make Him cold to grief. And notice the deep irony: the sign that gives life to Lazarus is the very thing that seals Jesus' death, and Caiaphas's cynical politics becomes an unwitting prophecy of the atonement.
basic.originalLanguages: The heart of the chapter is the claim ego eimi, I am the anastasis, the resurrection, and the zoe, the life. Jesus is not only the giver of resurrection life but its source in person. The sickness and the sign are for the doxa, the glory, of God, a glory that points ahead to the cross.
basic.typology: Lazarus called from the tomb is a sign and pledge of Jesus' own resurrection and of the final resurrection of all His people. The high priest's word that one must die for the people points to the true High Priest who dies to gather God's scattered children into one.
basic.christ: Christ is the resurrection and the life, who conquers death not merely by a miracle but in His own person. He weeps with the grieving and yet commands the grave. His raising of Lazarus prefigures His own rising, and it drives Him toward the cross where He will die for the people and for the scattered children of God.
basic.god: God is glorified in the Son, hears the Son always, and works even the enemies' plots into His saving purpose. The Father who sent the Son is displaying His glory in the defeat of death and preparing the greater glory of the cross.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 37 pictures God raising the dead to life. John 5 promised the hour when the dead hear the Son's voice. 1 Corinthians 15 proclaims Christ the firstfruits of resurrection. John 12 shows Lazarus's raising drawing crowds to Jesus.
basic.oneStory: Death, the last enemy since the fall, meets its master. Jesus, the resurrection and the life, calls a four-days-dead man from the tomb as a sign of His own coming victory. And the very sign that displays His power over death sets in motion His death for the people, through which the scattered children of God will be gathered into one.

context.literary:
John 11 is the longest continuous narrative in the Gospel after the passion, and it is built with great care around a rhythm of delay. The news arrives in verse 3, and the first thing Jesus does is nothing for two days, verse 6. Every later scene is a slow approach to the tomb: the conversation with the disciples, verses 7 to 16; Martha, 17 to 27; Mary, 28 to 37; the tomb itself, 38 to 44; and the council, 45 to 57. The reader is held back from the miracle as the characters are, and so feels the weight of the four days.

The chapter has a pointed symmetry between the two sisters. Martha meets Jesus on the road and speaks theology; Mary stays at home and then falls at His feet in tears. Both say the same words, 'Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died', verses 21 and 32, but the answers differ. To Martha Jesus gives a revelation, 'I am the resurrection and the life'. To Mary He gives no speech at all but goes with her to the grave, and weeps. John thus shows two ways in which the Lord meets grief, by teaching the mind and by sharing the sorrow.

The chapter is also full of references forward. Verse 2 names Mary as the one who 'was to anoint the Lord with perfume and wipe His feet with her hair', an event John only narrates in chapter 12. The grave clothes in verse 44 anticipate the cloths in the empty tomb of John 20:5-7. The words 'loud voice' recall 5:25 and 5:28. And the council's plan in verses 47 to 53 begins the final movement to the cross.

Irony runs throughout. Thomas says 'let us also go, so that we may die with Him', verse 16, not knowing how true it will be. The crowd asks whether the one who opened the eyes of the blind might have kept Lazarus from dying, verse 37, and the answer is that He will do more than that. And the council fears that if everyone believes, the Romans will take away 'our place and our nation', verse 48, when the death of Jesus is what will gather the nation and the scattered children. The chapter closes in Ephraim and at the edge of Passover, with everyone watching to see if He will come.
context.historical:
Bethany sat on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, a little less than two miles from Jerusalem, verse 18, and it was a place where Jesus was welcome. Luke 10:38-42 tells of Martha and Mary hosting Him in a village, and the family becomes a household of friends. The name Lazarus is a Greek form of Eleazar, which means 'God has helped'. The setting is near enough to the city that the leaders can hear what has happened within a day.

Mourning customs explain much of the scene. A death was followed by a quick burial, since the body was usually laid in a tomb on the day of death. Then came a period of loud mourning and visits from friends, and the Jews who have come from Jerusalem to console the sisters, verses 19 and 31, are part of that. The tomb is a cave with a stone across the entrance, verse 38, the usual family tomb cut into a hillside. The four days matter. Later rabbinic tradition held that the soul stays near the body for three days, hoping to return, and that by the fourth day corruption has set in. John is not discussing the tradition, but Martha's blunt remark that by now he stinks shows that the situation is past any ordinary hope.

The political situation is the real background of the chapter's ending. The council, the Sanhedrin, was the ruling body of Judea under the Romans, led by the high priest. Caiaphas held the office from AD 18 to 36 according to Josephus. The Romans allowed the priestly aristocracy to keep their position as long as they kept order, and a popular movement around a miracle worker risked exactly the kind of unrest that would invite Roman action. That is the fear in the phrase 'our place and our nation', verse 48. The chief priests belonged largely to the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, Acts 23:8, so the irony is complete: those who deny the resurrection plan the death of the one who has just raised a man.

Verses 54 to 57 show a nation approaching Passover. Pilgrims came early to purify themselves, as the Law required for those who had been defiled by contact with the dead, Numbers 9:6-10 and 19:11-13. Ephraim, a small town near the wilderness north of Jerusalem, is a place of retreat before the hour comes. The orders to report His whereabouts mark the beginning of a manhunt.
context.canonical:
The hope of resurrection grows slowly in the Old Testament, but it is there. Isaiah says, 'Your dead will live; their bodies will rise', Isaiah 26:19, and that the LORD 'will swallow up death forever', Isaiah 25:8. Daniel 12:2 says that many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, 'some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt'. Job looked for a Redeemer who would stand on the earth at the last and see God with his own eyes, Job 19:25-27. Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, Ezekiel 37, and God's promise to open the graves of His people, Ezekiel 37:12, give the image that stands behind Martha's hope of 'the resurrection at the last day', verse 24.

There are also actual raisings. Elijah restored the widow's son at Zarephath, 1 Kings 17:17-24, and Elisha raised the Shunammite's son, 2 Kings 4:32-37. In both cases the prophet cried to the LORD and stretched himself on the child. In the Gospels Jesus raises the daughter of Jairus, Mark 5:41-42, and the widow's son at Nain, Luke 7:11-17, with a simple word of command. The raising of Lazarus follows the pattern, but with a difference that John makes plain: the man has been dead four days, the scene is public, and the word is spoken in the name of the one who is Himself the resurrection.

John has already prepared for the claim. In chapter 5 Jesus said that the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and live, John 5:25-29. Lazarus is that hour on a small scale. The chapter then carries on into John 12, where the raising of Lazarus draws crowds, John 12:9-11, 17-18, and the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus as well.

In the rest of the New Testament Jesus' rising is the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the believers who have died have 'fallen asleep', 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14, the same image that Jesus uses in verse 11. In Revelation 1:18 the risen Lord says 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades'. The words of verse 25 stand behind the whole Christian confession of the resurrection.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John tells this story to bring his readers to the sentence that gives the sign its meaning: 'I am the resurrection and the life.' He means the reader to understand that the final hope of Israel, resurrection at the last day, has been brought into the present in a person, and that faith in Him is already a share in that life. The raising of Lazarus is not the point so much as the pointer. It is a sign, and signs in John exist so that people will believe and by believing have life in His name, John 20:30-31.

He also means to show who the Lord is by showing how He feels. The deliberate delay might read as coldness, but John tells us twice that Jesus loved the family, verses 3 and 5, and then He weeps. The reader is meant to hold together the majesty of the one who commands the grave and the tenderness of the one who goes to it in tears. This is the God that John is describing, and it was a word of comfort to churches that were burying their own dead.

John means as well to show the irony of the end. The sign that gives life to Lazarus produces the council that brings death to Jesus. Many believe, and some go straight to the Pharisees, verses 45 and 46. John does not mean to say that the miracle is a mistake; he wants readers to see that the very act of mercy makes the enemy strike. By putting Caiaphas's words in the mouth of an enemy and calling them a prophecy, John teaches that God governs even those who plot against Him. In the last paragraph, the reader should see that the death which the leaders plan for their own safety is the means by which the scattered children are gathered.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a unique event. Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead after four days, and Scripture does not tell believers to expect that those they love will be raised in the same way, or to pray for it as a rule. Many of those who prayed for the dying as Martha and Mary did saw them die. The account is a sign of a power that belongs to Christ and of the resurrection He will give at the end, not a promise of a particular outcome in each sickness. The comfort the chapter gives is not that death will always be reversed now, but that He is the resurrection and the life, and that death is not the last word for those who belong to Him.

The weeping of Jesus is descriptive and invites a response. Believers are not told that grief is unbelief. Paul writes that we do not grieve as those who have no hope, 1 Thessalonians 4:13, which does not mean that we do not grieve. If the Lord wept over a friend He was about to raise, grief at death is not a failure of faith.

Verse 4 is sometimes taken as a rule that every sickness is for God's glory, so that illness should be welcomed. It should not be. It says that in this case the sickness would not end in death but in God's glory. It is a word about Lazarus and about what Jesus was about to do. The verse does not forbid praying for healing or using medicine. Neither does it say that those who die of an illness have missed the glory of God.

What does carry forward as instruction is the call to believe and to obey at the tomb. 'Take away the stone,' Jesus says, and they do. 'Unwrap him and let him go,' He says, and the community is given a share in the work. The one who raises the dead asks His people to roll the stone and unbind the grave clothes, and that pattern of obedience still holds.

debates.question: What lay behind Jesus being 'deeply moved in spirit and troubled'?

views.label: Anger at death and its effects
views.case: The Greek word embrimaomai in verses 33 and 38 elsewhere carries a sense of strong displeasure, as when Jesus sternly warns those He has healed, Matthew 9:30 and Mark 1:43. On this reading Jesus is indignant at death, the enemy that has brought this grief, and at the unbelief He meets. Paul later calls death the last enemy, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and Hebrews 2:14-15 says Jesus came to break its power.

views.label: Deep sympathy for those who grieve
views.case: Others stress the context of weeping. Mary weeps, the Jews weep, and Jesus 'wept', verse 35. The verse says He was moved when He saw their tears. John adds that the bystanders say, 'See how He loved him!', verse 36, and the text raises no objection to that reading. The emotion is then one of compassion that shudders with the pain of those it loves.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Some argue that the two are not rivals. A person can be angry at a destroyer and sorrowful for its victims in the same moment, and the Greek words, which combine a physical shuddering with the troubling of His own spirit, suggest something larger than a single mood.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us what He was angry at, if He was angry, and so the safest conclusion is that the Lord is stirred in the presence of death. Whatever the exact shade, the lesson is the same: the Son of God does not regard death as natural or trivial, and He goes to it not as a spectator but with all His heart.

debates.question: What does 'whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies' and 'will never die' mean?

views.label: Physical death is not final
views.case: The first half of the saying speaks of the believer dying and yet living, and so it refers to the resurrection of those who die. Lazarus is the sign: he died and was called back. The final form of this promise is the rising of the dead at the last day, which Martha already believed, verse 24, and which Jesus holds out as present in Himself.

views.label: Spiritual death is ended
views.case: The second half, 'everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die', is for those who are alive. Since believers do in fact die, it must mean something more: that the life of God which believers now share is not touched by physical death. Jesus has already spoken of passing from death to life, John 5:24.

debates.bearing: The two halves belong together. The one who dies will live, and the one who lives by faith will not know the death that matters. Both are made secure by who Jesus is, and the test question is the one He asks Martha, 'Do you believe this?' Her answer is a confession of the person, not an explanation of the doctrine.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb embrimaomai in verses 33 and 38, translated 'deeply moved', is one of the strongest words for emotion in the Gospels. It is often said to have first described the snorting of horses, and elsewhere it carries a sense of stern rebuke or indignation, as in Mark 1:43 and Matthew 9:30. In verse 33 John pairs it with a second verb, tarasso, so that the Greek can be read as 'He troubled Himself'. The Lord's emotion is not something that overwhelms Him but something He takes on, which is in keeping with His control over the whole scene.

There are two different words for the weeping. Mary and the crowd weep with the verb klaio, the loud wailing of mourning, in verse 33. When Jesus weeps in verse 35, John uses a different verb, dakruo, 'to shed tears'. The difference may be a matter of quiet grief against public wailing, but at the very least it marks Jesus' tears as His own.

The word for 'asleep' in verse 11, koimao, is the ordinary biblical euphemism for death, as in Acts 7:60 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14. It carries the hope that sleep ends in waking. The disciples take it literally, and Jesus has to say plainly that Lazarus is dead. The pun matters, because Jesus says that He is going 'to wake him up', and that is exactly what He does.

Martha's confession in verse 27 uses the perfect tense: 'I believe', pepisteuka, which means 'I have come to believe and still do'. It is the settled faith of one who has already believed, and it comes before the sign. The titles she uses, the Christ, the Son of God, and the one who is coming into the world, gather the great hopes of the Gospel and are the same ones that John gives as the purpose of his book, John 20:31. Her response to 'Do you believe this?' is thus a model of the faith that precedes sight.

The call at the tomb is a short sentence in a loud voice, deuro exo, 'Lazarus, come out!' It is a simple summons, with no formula of prayer and no touch. The loud voice recalls the voice that the dead will hear, John 5:25 and 28. After it the man comes out still bound, and Jesus gives the command to the bystanders, 'Unwrap him and let him go', using the verbs luo and aphiemi, loose and release. The grave clothes are keiriai, strips of linen, with a soudarion, a cloth for the face, and these are the same terms that John uses in the account of Jesus' own burial and rising, John 20:5-7.

In verse 48 the council fears for 'our place and our nation', ton topon kai to ethnos. The word topos, 'place', can mean the temple, and this is the likely meaning. Caiaphas's reply uses the verb apothnesko, 'to die', with the preposition huper, 'on behalf of', and the same preposition is used of the good shepherd, 'for the sheep', John 10:11, and in 11:51 and 52 it is the language of substitution. John tells us that Caiaphas spoke not from himself, aph' heautou, but as high priest, and so was prophesying.

typology.type: Elijah and Elisha raising the dead
typology.fulfillment: Elijah stretched himself over the widow's son and cried to the LORD that the boy's life would return, 1 Kings 17:21, and Elisha did the same for the Shunammite's child, 2 Kings 4:32-37. These raisings show that God can give life back to the dead, and they stand in the Old Testament as signs of His power. In Jesus the correspondence becomes a contrast. The prophets pleaded with God and used their bodies; Jesus thanks the Father and calls with a word, Lazarus, come out, verses 41 to 43. The escalation is that He does not ask for the power but is the resurrection. The type falls short in that those raised died again, and so did Lazarus; only Christ's own rising is to a life that does not end.

God promised through Ezekiel, 'I will open your graves and bring you up from them', Ezekiel 37:12. The valley of dry bones was a picture of Israel's exile, and the promise was national restoration. Jesus has a man's grave opened and calls him up. The correspondence is the image of graves opened by God, and the New Testament takes it up when it says that all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son and come out, John 5:28-29. The escalation is from a vision of national renewal to a particular person called from a particular tomb. The type is still unfinished: the general resurrection of the last day remains ahead.

typology.type: The grave clothes of Lazarus and of Jesus
typology.fulfillment: Lazarus comes out bound in strips of linen with a cloth around his face, and needs others to set him free, verse 44. John later describes the clothes of Jesus: the linen cloths lie in the tomb, and the cloth that had been around His head is rolled up, lying separate, John 20:5-7. Lazarus was raised to come back to a life that would end; Jesus left the wrappings behind because He was not coming back to the old life but going on to the new. The correspondence is real, and the Gospel itself invites it by repeating the details. The escalation is from one who needs to be unbound to one who has left death behind, and the type falls short in that Lazarus is a sign but not the pattern of the glorified body.

typology.type: The high priest who prophesies the death of one for the nation
typology.fulfillment: Under the Law the high priest was the one who made atonement for the people on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:15-17, and what he did was a picture of a substitute standing for the nation. Caiaphas says that it is better that one man die for the people than that the nation perish, and John says that he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and for the scattered children of God, to gather them into one. The correspondence is the priest's role as a representative, spoken here by an unworthy priest. The escalation is that the true High Priest offers Himself, Hebrews 7:27 and 9:11-14. The type falls short in Caiaphas's own intent, which was political survival, and in the scope: Jesus' death is not for one nation but for the scattered of every nation.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ as the resurrection and the life, and its great gift is that it turns a doctrine into a person. Martha held the right belief, that her brother would rise at the last day, and Jesus does not correct it. He deepens it. 'I am the resurrection and the life.' The last day, with all its power, has stepped into the village of Bethany and is standing in front of her. Resurrection is not something He announces; it is something He is. Whoever is joined to Him by faith shares in His life, and a life that is His cannot be ended by death. That is why He asks her not 'Do you believe in the resurrection?' but 'Do you believe this?'

He is also the friend who weeps. The chapter does not hide the tension between His deliberate delay and His love, and it does not hide that He wept. Hebrews 4:15 says that we have a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, and Bethany is the plainest picture of what that means. He does not stand above the pain of death with a calm that has no feeling, and He does not weep as one without hope. He weeps and then He acts.

The sign leads straight to the cross. John makes the connection more bluntly here than anywhere else: the giving of life to Lazarus is the immediate cause of the plan to kill Jesus. The one who gives life to one friend will give His own life for many, and the reader is meant to see that the resurrection power He shows at the tomb is the power by which He will lay down His life and take it up again, John 10:17-18. At the cost of the sign He is on the road to the cross, and He knows it, which is why the disciples say in verse 8 that the Jews have just tried to stone Him and yet He goes. Thomas's line about dying with Him is more right than he knows.

Caiaphas's words are the Gospel in the mouth of an enemy. 'It is better for you that one man die for the people.' John adds that Jesus would die for the nation and also for the scattered children of God, to gather them into one, verses 51 and 52. The substitution, the scope and the purpose of His death are all stated here: one for many, from every nation, to gather into one. Paul will say that He died for all, 2 Corinthians 5:14-15.

His own rising is the proof of the claim. 'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. Lazarus was raised and died again; Jesus was raised and is the Living One, who holds the keys of Death and of Hades, Revelation 1:18. A caution applies. The strips of linen and the stone are not allegories to be decoded; the link to Christ rests on His own statements in the chapter and on the way the Gospel itself recalls these details at His own tomb.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all a God who delays and yet loves. The two things look opposed, and John does not soften the tension. 'Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days,' verses 5 and 6. The 'so' connects the love to the delay, not the delay to indifference. The Father's timing is not always the timing we ask for, and His love may be shown by waiting. This does not take away the sisters' grief or their honest complaint, 'if You had been here', which Jesus receives without rebuke. It does ask the reader to trust that a delay in God's purposes can serve a greater gift than the one requested.

God is glorified in the Son. 'This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it,' verse 4. The glory of the Father and of the Son are bound together. The glory here is not a spectacle but the display of who God is, and John will make plain that the glory of the Son comes by the cross, John 12:23-24. The raising of Lazarus shows God's glory in His power over death, and in the next hours it will show it in His love to the end.

God hears the Son always. 'Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. I knew that You always hear Me,' verses 41 and 42. The prayer at the tomb is brief and it is spoken aloud for the sake of the crowd, so that they may believe the Father sent Him. It reveals the unbroken communion between the Father and the Son, and it shows that the Son's miracles are not the work of a rival power but of the Father in the Son.

God is sovereign over His enemies. Caiaphas plots from fear and political calculation, and yet in saying what he says he becomes a spokesman for the very work of God, verses 49 to 52. Nothing the council does escapes the governing purpose of the Father, and the death they plan is the death He has appointed. The same truth is stated by the apostles later in Acts 4:27-28. God is not forced to cope with the plots of His enemies; He turns them into the means of the gospel.

God is the conqueror of death. The prophets promised that He would swallow up death forever and wipe the tears from every face, Isaiah 25:8, and Bethany is a first instalment of that promise, with tears wept and a tomb opened. Death, which came into the world through sin, is shown to be subject to the Son's word. Here is the answer to the question that the sisters and the crowds ask, 'Could not this man ... have kept Lazarus from dying?' He could, and He did something greater.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring our grief honestly to the Lord and to wait for His timing with trust. The God we worship hears our complaint, weeps with us, and commands the grave. Our praise is not an escape from sorrow but the confidence that the one who was moved by it is also the one who will end it.

crossReferences.note: Jesus said that the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. The call at the tomb, 'Lazarus, come out!', is the first public fulfilment on a small scale of that promise.

God will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from every face. The tears at Bethany and the opened tomb belong in the setting of this promise, and the raising of Lazarus is a sign of the day when the promise is completed.

God says that He will open the graves of His people and bring them up. The image lies behind Martha's belief in the resurrection at the last day, and the opening of the tomb of Lazarus is a picture of what God will do for all His people.

Elijah cried to the LORD and the boy's life returned to him. It is the closest Old Testament parallel to the raising of Lazarus, and the difference is that Jesus does not plead for the power to raise the dead but speaks as the one who is the resurrection.

At Nain Jesus touched the coffin and said, 'Young man, I tell you, get up!' It shows that the raising of Lazarus was not an isolated case, and that a word from Jesus was enough to bring the dead back to life.
The chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well. It shows the unreasoning fear that follows the sign, and it makes the point that the living evidence of Jesus' power is itself seen as a threat.

The cloth that had been around Jesus' head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths. The details of burial at the tomb of Lazarus return here, and the contrast between the bound man and the empty cloths marks the difference between a raising and a resurrection.

Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Lazarus is a sign of the harvest, and Christ's own rising is the firstfruits that guarantees it for all who belong to Him.
We have a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses and who was without sin. The weeping of Jesus at the tomb is the clearest picture in the Gospels of this sympathy.

The risen Lord says that He was dead and now is alive forever and ever, and that He holds the keys of Death and of Hades. The claim of verse 25 is here seen in its final form: the one who is the resurrection holds the keys of the grave.

Paul says that we do not grieve like those who have no hope, because God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him. It takes the image of sleep from verse 11 and makes it the basis of Christian comfort.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's account of death begins in a garden with a warning and a sentence. 'You will surely die', Genesis 2:17, and then, 'to dust you shall return', Genesis 3:19. From that point every grave in Scripture is an echo of the first, and the genealogies of Genesis 5 repeat their refrain, 'and then he died'. Death is the great enemy of the human story, and the Bible does not treat it as natural. Lazarus's tomb is the place where the story's oldest sorrow is met by its oldest promise.

Through the Old Testament the promise grows. A woman in Zarephath and another in Shunem receive their sons back, and the prophets see a day when God will swallow up death forever. Daniel sees the dust-sleepers awake. Yet these hopes remain in the future, and Martha speaks for generations of believers when she says, 'I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.' The story has been waiting for someone who can say more.

At Bethany it says more. The hope of the last day is placed in a person who is standing on the road, and who speaks and a dead man walks out. The sign is a small piece of the end brought to the middle. It is also a hinge in the story, because the sign is what finally leads the leaders to decide to kill Jesus. The cross that will break the power of death is set in motion by the raising of a friend, and the gathering of the scattered children of God, a thread that begins at Babel and runs through the prophets' hope for the return, is attached to His death in the mouth of Caiaphas.

The story ends where death itself ends. Paul says that the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and John sees the new heaven and the new earth, where God will dwell with His people and 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain', Revelation 21:3-4. The tears of Bethany are the last tears. The voice that called Lazarus by name will call all His people, and the garden that was lost to death is replaced by a city where the tree of life grows, and death is no more.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus stay two more days before going to Lazarus?

options.text: So that God would be glorified and the disciples would believe, through a greater sign than healing.
options.note: Verses 4 and 15 give the purpose: the glory of God and the disciples' faith.

options.text: Because He did not really care about the family.
options.note: Verse 5 says He loved them; the delay was purposeful love, not indifference.

options.text: Because He was afraid to return to Judea.
options.note: The disciples raised the danger, but Jesus chose to go; fear was not His reason for waiting.

options.text: So that a greater miracle of resurrection could reveal who He is.
options.note: True, but it omits the stated aims, the glory of God and the disciples' belief.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by I am the resurrection and the life?

options.text: Resurrection and life are found in His own person, so those who believe in Him live even though they die.
options.note: Verses 25 and 26 make Jesus Himself the source of resurrection life, not just a future event.

options.text: He will one day raise the dead at the last day and nothing more.
options.note: Martha already believed in a last-day resurrection; Jesus reveals He is the resurrection now, in person.

options.text: He promises a good afterlife to those who are moral.
options.note: The promise is life through faith in Him, not a reward for morality.

options.text: Those who trust Him receive life that death cannot end.
options.note: True, but it does not capture the striking claim that He Himself is the resurrection and the life.

quiz.q: What is significant about Jesus weeping at the tomb?

options.text: His power over death does not make Him cold; He enters fully into human grief.
options.note: Verse 35 shows the compassion of the one who is about to raise the dead.

options.text: He wept because He was powerless to help.
options.note: He was about to raise Lazarus; His tears were grief, not helplessness.

options.text: He wept chiefly so the crowd would see His love.
options.note: The onlookers did say see how He loved him, but His tears were genuine grief, not a performance.

options.text: He shared in the sorrow of those who mourned.
options.note: True, but it understates the striking union of real grief with the power that was about to conquer death.

quiz.q: What was the result of the raising of Lazarus among the leaders?

options.text: They convened the Sanhedrin and resolved to kill Jesus.
options.note: Verses 47 to 53 record the plot that followed the sign.

options.text: They repented and believed in Him.
options.note: Many of the people believed, but the leaders plotted His death.

options.text: They acknowledged the sign but refused to believe.
options.note: They could not deny the sign, yet rather than believe they resolved to kill Him.

options.text: They feared the people would follow Him and Rome would act.
options.note: True of their reasoning, but it omits the decisive outcome, that they plotted to kill Him.

quiz.q: What deeper truth lay in Caiaphas's words that one man should die for the people?

options.text: Though he meant cold politics, he unwittingly prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation and gather the scattered children of God into one.
options.note: Verses 51 and 52 reveal the prophecy hidden in his cynical statement.

options.text: He sincerely understood and proclaimed the gospel of the atonement.
options.note: He did not understand; John says God made his self-serving words an unwitting prophecy.

options.text: He was simply making a practical political calculation with no deeper meaning.
options.note: John explicitly says he was prophesying, though he did not grasp it.

options.text: He rightly stated that Jesus' death would benefit the people.
options.note: True in the words themselves, but it misses that this was an unwitting prophecy pointing to the atonement for Jew and Gentile.

questions: Jesus delayed out of love, to give a greater gift. When God seems slow to answer, how might His delay be working a deeper good than the quick help you wanted?
Jesus asked Martha, do you believe this, right at the graveside. How would you answer that question in the face of your own losses?
Jesus wept even though He knew He would raise Lazarus. How does it comfort you that Christ enters your grief rather than brushing it aside?
The sign that gave Lazarus life led Jesus toward His own death. How does it deepen your worship to see that your life came at the cost of His?
Jesus called a dead man by name, and he came out. Where do you need to hear the life-giving voice of Christ calling you out of deadness today?

translationNotes.note: A little less than two miles renders the Greek measure; the BSB footnote gives about fifteen stadia, roughly 1.72 miles. Bethany's nearness to Jerusalem explains the official attention the sign drew.
Deeply moved in spirit; the BSB footnote notes it can be rendered He was indignant in spirit, also in verse 38. Jesus' emotion mingles grief with holy anger at death itself.
Four days in the tomb was understood to place death beyond any doubt, heightening the wonder of the raising.
John explains that Caiaphas, as high priest, unwittingly prophesied Jesus' substitutionary death for the nation and for the scattered children of God, gathered into one.
